claims: Appendicitis is a medical emergency.
Appendicitis is caused by an inflamed appendix.
Appendicitis is usually triggered by a blockage.
Appendicitis results in sudden, severe abdominal pain that often moves from the belly button to the lower-right abdomen.
Vomiting is a symptom of appendicitis.
Loss of appetite is a symptom of appendicitis.
Abdominal tenderness is a symptom of appendicitis.
Pain of appendicitis often begins around the belly button.
Pain of appendicitis shifts to the lower right abdomen.
Pain of appendicitis worsens with movement, coughing, or walking.
Nausea is a symptom of appendicitis.
Constipation is a symptom of appendicitis.
Diarrhea is a symptom of appendicitis.
Low-grade fever is a symptom of appendicitis.
Abdominal bloating is a symptom of appendicitis.
Inability to pass gas is a symptom of appendicitis.
Pain of appendicitis may differ in children or during pregnancy.
Hardened stool (fecaliths) is the most common cause of appendicitis.
Fecaliths block the opening of the appendix.
Lymphoid hyperplasia is a cause of blockage leading to appendicitis.
Lymphoid hyperplasia is swollen lymphoid tissue.
Lymphoid hyperplasia often follows a viral infection.
Colitis or tumors are other sources of obstruction or infection leading to appendicitis.
Obstruction of the appendix causes bacteria to multiply.
Obstruction of the appendix leads to swelling.
Obstruction of the appendix leads to pus.
Obstruction of the appendix can lead to rupture.
Physical exam for appendicitis checks for pain in the lower right abdomen.
Blood and urine tests for appendicitis check for infection or pregnancy.
Abdominal ultrasound is commonly used to confirm inflammation in appendicitis diagnosis.
CT scan is commonly used to confirm inflammation in appendicitis diagnosis.
Appendicitis is most common in people aged 10–30.
Appendicitis is slightly more common in males.
Family history of appendicitis can increase risk.
Appendectomy is the standard treatment for appendicitis.
Appendectomy is surgery to remove the appendix.
Antibiotics are sometimes used for appendicitis.
Surgery is preferred to prevent rupture in appendicitis treatment.
An infected appendix can rupture in 48–72 hours if left untreated.
Rupture spreads infection in the abdomen (peritonitis).
Peritonitis can be fatal.
